If I understand correctly, method="trust-constr" is considered to be the most modern, highest-quality, and currently-best-supported of the strategies available for scipy.optimize.minimize() when doing constrained minimization. In particular, it's the only method that supports both constraints and analytic gradient and hessian. But I am having trouble getting reasonable accuracy from it. Its accuracy is low by default (roughly single precision), which is fine, but I haven't succeeded in finding settings to get it much better than that. My simple test example problem is to find the local minimum of y=cos(x) near x=3, with no constraints. That local minimum occurs at x=pi, y=-1. If I'm not mistaken, this example problem is well-conditioned (locally well-approximated by a quadratic), so I expect the solve to go simply and smoothly-- there's not much to it. The larger "real" problems I am trying to solve are similar to this, generally with equality constraints (so this limits which solver strategies I can use; "trust-constr" is one of the few). I often don't have inequality constraints. The objective functions are "nice" in the sense that they have a quadratic basin around the desired local minimum. Further details of my much-more-complicated real-life objective functions and equality constraints aren't relevant here-- the accuracy problem with trust-constr is shown clearly by cos(x) without needing any constraints at all. The program below tries 20 or so different initial guesses between 2.0 and 4.0, with aggressive tolerance settings agnostic to whether there are constraints and/or bounds: gtol,xtol,barrier_tol all set to 1e-20 (the default for all three is 1e-8). The answers from scipy have relative error as high as 3e-9 (i.e. slightly better than single precision accuracy). On this well-conditioned input, I expected something on the order of 1e-15 (double-precision accuracy). For comparison, the program also contains a little Newton's-method solver. Given the same information as was given to scipy.optimize.minimize() (the gradient and hessian, asking it to find where the gradient is zero) the Newton solver always converges to exactly the right answer (to machine precision) math.pi, in 7 or fewer iterations, as expected, on each of the initial guesses. I expect 'trust-constr' to be able to do this too. Am I doing something wrong in my usage of scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') ? I guess I could code up my own constrained-minimizer from first principles using Newton's method and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier . But I thought scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') was supposed to be a state-of-the-art implementation of that and more... isn't it? Alternatively, I could use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') to get a coarse approximation of the answer, and then use Newton's method to polish the answer. However, given that Newton's method is only a handful of lines of code (even with Lagrange multipliers added), I'm surprised if scipy can't do that itself. Is the accuracy of scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') really this limited? Or am I missing some settings that will make it do better? #!/usr/bin/python3 import math import scipy import warnings max_newton_iterations_ever = 0 def simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(f, df, initial_guess): # { global max_newton_iterations_ever print(f" in simple_newton_solver_for_comparison") x = initial_guess for i in range(100): max_newton_iterations_ever = max(max_newton_iterations_ever, i+1) fx = f(x) dfx = df(x) newx = x - fx/dfx print(f" i={i}: {x} - {fx}/{dfx} -> {newx}") if newx == x: print(f" (which is the same as previous, so converged)") break #
